articles.title: THE EFFECT OF BEHOLDING THE LORD’S GLORY
articles.author: R. Hibbert

paragraphs.text: What is in mind in reading these scriptures is the advantage of entering into surroundings of glory in company with Christ and the bearing of that on our testimonial activities. As we have been reminded, the service of God includes much more than we generally have in mind in speaking of it, that is, what engages us after the Lord comes in at the Supper. One’s suggestion is that we are qualified to have effective part in the testimony as we are formed by the experiences of being in the company of Christ in the area of glory.

So the Lord selected these great men, in view of their education. You might say, ‘Why did He not take the whole twelve?’. Well, that is an important matter. We learn everything from Christ, and why should He select three? Why should He not? He had a perfect right to select three. He selected these same three on three very important occasions. What are we to learn from that? We are to learn that the Lord has sovereign rights to select whom He will in His testimony. So we need to be warned against any idea of democracy in the assembly.

I think we are in danger of modifying the thought of selection. But the Lord has His rights to select certain persons in His testimony and to distinguish them. That is His right. He said, “Is it not lawful for me to do what I will in my own affairs?”, Matthew 20: 15. It is not only a right but it is also for the good of the brethren. So we should be very thankful if we see the marks of the Lord’s selection in some of our beloved brethren because it is for the enrichment of the assembly and for the blessing of the saints. I just touch on that because I think it is a current matter that we need to be on our guard against a kind of levelling idea that has been brought in because of certain sorrowful matters in the past, but we must be balanced in that as in everything.

Matthew is the royal gospel, the King in His beauty—there is a book on that. If the young brethren want to read it, they will find it very enjoyable, very instructive (J.T., N.S. Vol. 11, p.250). Speaking to the young brethren I would say this—I remember that when I first used to come to the meetings the ministry was Greek to me. I did not know what the brethren were talking about. I used to think, ‘I do not think I will ever understand’; but I started to get interested and I started to read the ministry, and you know there is a saying that the appetite comes while eating, and that is very true in connection with ministry, that the more you read of it the more your taste for it will grow. Get into the habit of taking up the ministry and reading it constantly. The constancy of it is more important than the quantity. So there is no need to be afraid—that is a very fine word in this section, the Lord says, “Be not terrified”.

Here in Matthew’s gospel, when He is presented in all His royal majesty in circumstances of glory, it says, they were “greatly terrified. And Jesus coming to them touched them, and said, Rise up, and be not terrified”. Well, that is a fine thing in the presence of absolute authority. It is that which Matthew presents. It is the King in His beauty, but it is the King in His authority.

It has been pointed out that a characteristic word in Matthew is ‘go’. In the army an officer does not say, ‘Will you please do so-and-so’. He says, ‘You do that’. That is an order, and is what characterises Matthew’s gospel. ‘Go’, He says, there are no arguments. You do not argue with a king, it is a royal command. We need to be reminded too that divine principles are not flexible, they are not modified by circumstances. Persons sometimes bring in reasons why they should be modified and say there are ifs and buts, and sympathies, and so on. But divine principles are not changeable, or adaptable to any particular opinions or circumstances; ‘situational ethics’ have no place in the assembly.

I would recommend to the brethren who have not read it (I hope every one here has) that classic letter by Dr. Pavlik. What was of great help to me was that he said, in going over the histories of the divisions, that in spite of personalities, in spite of devoted men getting wrong, God always supported those who followed divine principles. I think that would be a great cue to us, that instead of getting confused by personal sympathies and details, we see what the principle is and then we say, ‘That is it; that is the divine commandment’. You say, Is that christianity? Yes, it is christianity, and just as true as it was in the Old Testament. It is not a question of legality, but it is a question of principles, and christianity is supported by principles, divine principles, that cannot be modified for anyone. That is Matthew’s line.

So in Matthew it is a question of the word. What is inflexible in this sense is that there is no modification of the word of God. The Scriptures are absolute. There is nothing else to compare with them. If you have got a scripture you may have to be careful about that too, because a lot of people wrongly claim scriptural ground, but Scripture understood in the power of the Spirit is to be obeyed, and obeyed without any question. So if we have a scripture that rightly governs a matter, that settles it for the spiritual mind and the subject mind. That is, there is no need for any more dispute or waiting. So the great thing is to find out what scripture applies.

Many have gone astray on this very point, but it is essential that we should learn this, that the Lord is in charge and if He says a certain thing, if He establishes a certain matter from the Scriptures, it is final. He says Himself that His words will in no wise pass away (Matthew 24: 35). There is no change in them; they are absolute.
That will simplify so much difficulty if we can see what is the divine principle that governs a matter. Then we need not be terrified. ‘Oh’, you may say, ‘how is that going to affect me?

How is it going to affect my relatives? What is it going to cost me?’. The principle of associations comes into these three scriptures in the references to His garments. How is that going to affect me? That is the way that we think humanly—what is it going to cost me? Can I afford to face up to the truth? It is very fine that in this gospel, where the Lord is in full command and in the full dignity of royalty, it says, “The disciples hearing it fell on their faces, and were greatly terrified. And Jesus coming to them touched them, and said, Rise up, and be not terrified”. It is very affecting that in His dignity and royalty there should be this element of compassion. That comes into Matthew, “Behold thy King cometh … meek, and mounted upon an ass, and upon a colt the foal of an ass” (Matthew 21: 5). That is the kind of King we have: He is sympathetic and He is comforting and yet He is, none the less, the King.

Now in Mark there is a difference. The stress in Mark would be on ‘hear’, “Hear him”. I have often wondered why this is all God said on that occasion, “This is my beloved Son—hear him”. What is involved in that? Certainly it is not lengthy. Mark is a prophetic gospel. We do not want long sermons in prophetic meetings; we want short words that are pertinent and applicable. I have spoken about Matthew and there it says, “He cast out the spirits with a word” (Matthew 8: 16), just a word. That was all that was needed. He did not need to handle those persons, a word was enough. In fact one man said, “I am not fit that thou shouldest enter under my roof; but only speak a word, and my servant shall be healed”, Matthew.8: 8.
Just the word; authoritative ministry is really the Scripture applied in the power of the Spirit so that it is evidently a word from the Lord.

Mark’s gospel is marked not just by speaking, but by the Lord touching and handling persons. Of the leper it says He freely handled him (see note to Mark 1: 41), not just that He touched him. There is the deaf man, where He put His fingers to his ears (Mark 7: 32–35).

That is different from sending a message a long distance. In Mark He gets near to people and He handles persons, even a leper. He is able to handle him and then He takes the deaf man out and puts His fingers to his ears. Now what does that mean? think it is an instruction for us how to serve in prophetic meetings, how a prophet would serve. He would not simply send a word at a distance, he would get to know the conditions involved and get near sympathetically and form a kind of ‘rapport’ with his audience. I think the brethren will understand what I mean by that word. If you are speaking in a ministry meeting can you see you are effecting something? Samson, when he went to deal with those Philistines said to the lad that held him by the hand, “Suffer me to feel the pillars”, Judges 16: 26. Now in prophetic ministry you can do that. If you are with the Lord you can feel the pillars; you can feel what needs to be brought down, what needs to be removed, what needs to be effected, and that means establishing a rapport with your audience.
Prophetic ministry is directed to the conscience, and it is a great need at the present time.

There are current issues amongst us that authority is not quite enough to meet. You can point out the principle endlessly, but it may not make any difference; but can you get to the persons and affect them by contact? That is the thing with Mark. You remember the prophet Elisha when the dead boy’s mother went to him. He said, I will send my servant with my staff—and it did not do any good (2 Kings 4: 25–37). The authority did not effect anything; so he goes and lies upon the child to give warmth and impart what will effect something. That is what I think prophetic ministry is intended to do.
The sisters come into this. There are a good many here, thank God, and the sisters have a very great place. Scripture distinctly refers to sisters prophesying and refers to prophetesses.

It does not refer to priestesses, though sisters are priests. It refers to queens and it refers to prophetesses and to a shepherdess. So I think that in some of our local concerns the answer may be coming through the sisters, feeling sisters who are carrying things and who perhaps can wisely say a brief word in private. Now that is very important

for all. Prophetic words should be pointed and potent and brief—“Five words with my understanding”, 1 Corinthians 14: 19. Five words are better than ten thousand words. Think of listening to ten thousand words! That would be a test, would it not? I do not know how long that would take, but there would not be much room for a number two—or a number three, if necessary, which is sometimes doubtful.

Now we come to Luke. What is distinctive about Luke is that it says, “as he prayed”. You might say that Luke stresses the Lord’s knees. Matthew stresses His word, and Mark stresses His hands, he records, “Such works of power are done by his hands”, Mark 6: 2. You can see that involves more than words. But what can be done by prayer! The Lord, of course, is the example here. It says that “the fashion of his countenance became different”. What can happen to us in prayer! how you can be changed yourself in prayer, to begin with, how you can become different, come out differently. You go into God one way and you come out with some change. If you are really in contact with God there is going to be some change. But then what change can be effected in others by one as changed!

I think, beloved brethren, that there are matters among us that are causing universal concern that are only going to be settled through the greater exercise of urgent prayer, urgent crying to God. That is what Luke presents. You may say, Is that glorious? This is in the glory on the mount, and the true glory of manhood is dependence. That is what God delights to see in persons, dependence; not people who can quote a lot of precedents and pride themselves on their historical knowledge of things in the testimony. I do not know that God will get much out of that, but God loves to see a

dependent man. He loves to welcome into His presence a man who is marked by prayer. This was characteristic of the Lord. Luke is the only gospel where it says that in Gethsemane the Lord knelt down. Think of the Lord kneeling down, praying to God. And it says that “being in conflict he prayed more intently”, Luke 22: 44. What a way to pray when we are in conflict! Do we pray the more intently when in conflict? If you have some difficulty with someone, how do you try to meet that? We see how the Lord met the situation when He was in direct conflict with Satan. Satan was trying to impede His determination to carry out God’s will, and the Lord, speaking reverently, was there in weakness, human weakness. It says that an angel appeared from heaven strengthening Him.

This is a great encouragement because perhaps every time you stand up to serve the brethren your knees tremble. That is felt weakness, but we do not need to be afraid of that. Paul said, “When I am weak, then I am powerful”, 2 Corinthians 12: 10. So it is an advantage. It is far better to get up feeling very dependent than it would be to get up feeling quite independent.

You could not count on support on that line. So you could say that the knees are what characterised the Lord in Luke. He went to the mount of Olives “as was his custom”, that is, it was characteristic. It is not just turning to God when we are in a difficult spot. Think of the Lord praying all night. But it says, “as was his custom”. And in our scripture, “And as he prayed the fashion of his countenance became different and his raiment white and effulgent”.

Well, as the brethren know, there is nothing about the mount of transfiguration in John, except that you might say the whole book is that. But what I would say simply is this—the Lord is an example in these three instances on the mount, and He is an example in John, not in relation to His word exactly, not exactly in relation to His handling persons, and not exactly in relation to praying, but in relation to the bosom. That is what characterises John. That is the place that is alluded to, Christ is in the bosom of the Father, and then John in His bosom is the characteristic man in John’s gospel.
So that is the place where we can get help, where we can get revelations, where we can enjoy communion, and an area out of which we can come in power to meet things in the testimony.

Then He says, “I have given you an example that, as I have done to you, ye should do also”, John 13: 15. He had just been speaking about part with Him, and that is what my subject is, part with the Lord in the testimony, how we can carry on our area in the testimony in the spirit that the Lord did. Oh, you may say, I thought part with Him was in approaching the Father, and so it is, but it is quite evident from what the Lord has to say in that section that He has Peter especially in mind, and the others, in testimony here; He says, “I have given you an example that, as I have done to you, ye should do also”. And what is the example? The example is humility. I believe that if there is one issue more than any other that the Lord has had with us it is pride, it is lack of humility. So think of the Lord having to show them that.

Think of Him taking a wash-hand basin, getting down at the disciples’ feet, and He is saying, If you are not ready for this, well then, you are ruled out. Peter objected to it. It does not appeal to us much, but that is the way the Lord leaves the example. “I have given you an example that, as I have done to you, ye should do also”. He says to Peter, If you are not ready for that, then you cannot have part with Me.

We want to have part with Him, beloved brethren, in what we have had before us earlier in Psalm 45, in that glorious service, but we also want to have part with Him in this practical side of the service, in every area that has to do with the things of God, to have the Lord before us as an example and to be like Him and to be formed by the experiences that we enjoy as we are with Him in circumstances of glory, so that we can bring the effect of that, the formation that results from that, to circumstances down here that in themselves are not glorious, but that the glory can meet. May God bless the word.

I wanted to speak about these three men of whom we have read; this young man of Egypt, the younger son, and Judas. These were all persons who at one time had a certain value. The young man of Egypt was the servant of an Amalekite. No doubt he had served him well; he had come far with him, right from Egypt into the land of Judah, and he had been a profitable servant it would seem. Then he fell sick. He no longer had any value, and he was simply abandoned. This is what the world does with people who serve it. For a time they have value, they are of use, and then when they have served their turn they are simply cast aside. The Lord never does that with anyone. The Lord Jesus preserves
and maintains those who serve Him, and in the glad tidings He is seeking to recover and to save, and then to use, those who put their trust in Him.

So here we have this young man found in a field. What a wretched plight he was in, left there without any resources whatsoever, left in his sickness, in his distress, just left to his own devices, with no one to help him. But he is found by the servants of David and brought to him. So we can be thankful for those who have care for our souls. Some of us have experience of the service of others, finding us where we were and bringing us to Christ. This is what we would seek to do in the glad tidings. If there are any here who do not know Jesus, we would like to bring you to Him, we would like you to prove for yourself what a Master He is. The first thing David does for this young man is to see that he is fed, and then he raises these questions with him. So the Lord would feed us and see to it that we are nourished, giving us to understand that He cares for us and has an interest in us.

So David raises these questions with him—“To whom belongest thou? and whence art thou?”—good questions for each one of us to ponder and to answer. “To whom belongest thou?” Do we belong to Jesus? Each one of us belongs to someone and it is a good thing to belong to Jesus. The apostle says, “Ye are not your own … for ye have been bought with a price”, 1 Corinthians 6: 19, 20. The Lord Jesus desires to have us for Himself; He is seeking to set free captives to sin and Satan; He would delight to set us free from these other influences and attach us to Himself. Do we all know that we belong to Jesus? Do we all know Him as our Saviour and Lord? David asks this of the young man and he is able to give an account of himself. Then he becomes of value to David; he is used to bring him down to the troop

and thus everything is recovered. It is a good thing to be set free from the world which has cast Christ off, cast Him aside as worthless. He is “the stone which the builders cast away as worthless” (1 Peter 2: 7); there is no place for Jesus in this world. He did not fit into the world system; there was no place for Him. Even when He came in as a Babe, there was no room for Him in the inn. He was born in conditions of privation, and cradled in a manger.
Think of that—the One who made the world coming into His own creation and there being no room for Him!

Well, this young man no doubt felt keenly the fact that he had been cast aside, but as he came into touch with David he would find a master of very different character, one who would care for him and cherish him, one whose affection would be displayed and one who would claim his affections. The great thing about David was that he attracted people and held them by reason of their affection for him. In Saul’s system there was harshness, there was demand. In the system of many of the kings that followed David there was the same feature of demand and extortion. But David was one who had always something to contribute to his own. We have been reminded often that he never lost a battle. This particular point where we have read was perhaps the lowest point in his fortunes, but it says later in the chapter that “David recovered all” (1 Samuel 30: 18).

So the Lord Jesus is going to retain, feed, and care for any one who puts his trust in Him. I would say to the young people here, and to us all, let us put our trust in Jesus; and let us see the true character of the world, a harsh, demanding system which has a use for people only so long as they can serve it, but when they have served their turn they are simply cast aside.
How often you have seen it

happen; you see it in business, you see it—in politics; great statesmen who have served their turn are rejected and forgotten about. But in the great christian system the Lord Jesus cares for every one of us and He delights to have us serve Him. So let us appreciate the fact that persons have a care for our souls and can put us in touch with the Saviour In Luke 15 we read about this well-known younger son, one who was in the father’s house but felt he was being deprived of something. When he was there he was sheltered from the world and did not know the sort of place it was; he never had to look for anything, all was provided for him. But he rather tired of what he thought was the restriction of his father’s house. Sometimes, you know, those of us who have been brought up in christian households chafe a little at what we think of as restrictions. We may feel we would like to taste what the world has to offer, to see something different and do something different, just as this young man did. So his father allows him to go this distance. He divided to his sons what he was possessed of, and this young man goes off. For a time he proves to be very popular and has many friends; he has all that his heart desires. But the end result is that he spends everything, he “dissipate his property, living in debauchery”. What a sorry plight he is now in, left with nothing but the unhappy memory of his folly. A violent famine arose throughout the country and he began to be in want, and nobody gave anything to him. No doubt he went around his friends to see what they would do for him, and he very soon found the answer. They would not do anything. He finds himself in servitude he finds himself in this loathsome position, longing to fill his belly with the husks which the swine were eating.
Then it says that “coming to himself, he said,

How many hired servants of my father’s have abundance of bread”. What a good thing it is, if we get away on our own course, that we come to ourselves, that we remember things. How many must have memories of happier times and happier experiences which they once enjoyed. We would long that persons might come to themselves, those who have gone away from what they know to be right. Oh that they might remember where there is full provision for them, just as this young man did.

So he comes to himself and goes back. He has made up in his mind this little speech, what he is going to say to his father and what he is going to ask for—a place among the servants. But when he is yet a long way off he finds that his father has been looking out for him, runs to meet him, and embraces him; and instead of giving him the place of a servant he restores him fully to what he previously enjoyed—and far more. That is a great thing about christianity, that things are preserved for us, things are kept; there is always somewhere where the truth is preserved, there are always persons who are seeking to go on with what is right. I am sure that those of us who believe we are in the pathway of faith would seek to preserve things for persons who may come to themselves and return to where the blessing is, to where the Father’s love is known, where nothing has ever failed.

So that is the wonderful message of the glad tidings. If we return, everything is once more available to us. What a contrast between the condition of this young man in the fields feeding swine, with nothing to eat, and his being received back into his father’s house, clothed with the best robe, a ring on his hand, feet shod, feasting on the best that could be provided. What a God we have, beloved! Let us prove Him more; let us draw more

abundantly on what He has, and let us appreciate more fully the blessing that is ours in having to do with such a glorious Provider. One who has provided everything for us. “He who, yea, has not spared his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, how shall he not also with him grant us all things?”, Romans 8: 32.

In Matthew’s gospel we have this very solemn and unique picture, because Judas is a unique character, one who knew the Lord intimately, we would judge from the Psalms, where he is referred to as “mine own familiar friend”, Psalm 41: 9. How close he, must have been to Jesus; they “held sweet intercourse together. To the house of God we walked amid the throng”, Psalm 55: 14. Judas was evidently close to the Lord and trusted by the other disciples. Right up to the time when he betrayed the Lord it would seem that the other disciples did not suspect the character of Judas. The Lord, of course—knew who would deliver Him up; He knows everything about every one of us. John’s gospel tells us that He did not trust Himself to man because “Himself knew what was in man”, John 2: 25. He knows every one of us through and through; nothing is hidden from the searching and watchful eyes of the Lord Jesus, for His eyes are as a flame of fire. Everything is discerned, weighed, measured and evaluated by Him. So He knew Judas. Judas, close as he was to Jesus, was beguiled by the lure of money, and had gone to the chief priests and offered to deliver up Jesus. We are told elsewhere that when he went there they rejoiced. They were glad to see Judas because he could help them to accomplish their evil purpose. No doubt Judas was made very welcome; he would be a very popular man. And anyone who would seek to betray the Lord will for a time be popular.
Think of what remorse must have filled the soul

of Judas as he contemplated what he had done. The act which he perpetrated was without parallel; to sell and to betray the Son of God, the Lord of glory. Judas might well be filled with remorse. Many persons who have gone on a wrong course have been filled with remorse, but we are not to confuse remorse with repentance. You remember how Esau, when he had sold his birthright, was remorseful, but it says, “he found no place for repentance”, Hebrews 12: 17. What the Lord is looking for with us is repentance, “repentance towards God, and faith towards our Lord Jesus Christ”, Acts 20: 21. Those are the terms of the glad tidings.
‘Repentance only. God requires from man,
And faith in Christ, His well beloved Son’.

That is all we have to do, that is the simple message of the glad tidings. How profound a thing it is to repent, to acknowledge our sins and feel the weight and burden of them; to feel how unable we are to do anything about them, and just to realise that Jesus has done everything for us.

Judas was filled with remorse and he went to the chief priests, seeking in some way, I suppose, to salve his conscience. But there was no alleviation for him. He found that, having done what the chief priests and elders required of him, they had no further use for him. “What is that to us?”, they say, “see thou to that”. What a solemn contemplation! Here was a man who had done the foulest deed that could be imagined, and all that remains for him is to go and hang himself. He went “to his own place”, Acts 1: 25.

It underlines for us what the character of the world is, whether it be the religious world as in the case of Judas, the social world, as the younger son found, or the commercial world, or whatever it might be, that the young Egyptian had experienced.
Once a person has served his turn the world has no further use for him.

I wanted to contrast that with what we have set out in the second epistle to Timothy. This is a passage which was written by Paul towards the end of his pathway. So we think of Paul here as an old man, one who had served much and suffered many things for the sake of Jesus; one who had faithfully fulfilled the mission that was committed to him. What a vessel Paul was!

Here he is in prison and has the consciousness that he has come to the end of his pathway. He says, “For I am already being poured out, and the time of my release is come”. Well, the Lord did not desert him. He says, “At my first defence no man stood with me, but all deserted me.

May it not be imputed to them. But the Lord stood with me, and gave me power, that through me the proclamation might be fully made, and all those of the nations should hear; and I was delivered out of the lion’s mouth. The Lord shall deliver me from every wicked work, and shall preserve me for his heavenly kingdom”, 2 Timothy 4: 16–18. What a contrast with what the world would do to persons who have served it! The Lord will never desert His own; He will stand with them right to the end. He would give us the consciousness of His being interested in every one of us here, desiring our welfare, our well-being and our blessing, desiring to comfort and sustain us and bring us through. This is a comfort to all of us, young and old alike, that the Lord Jesus will be with us. His own promise is, “I am with you all the days, until the completion of the age”, Matthew 28: 20.
So Paul, this old man, was writing to a young man. Timothy. He can say what his own experience has been, and he can point Timothy, and all of us,

to what the Lord has laid up for us. “Henceforth the crown of righteousness is laid up for me, which the Lord, the righteous Judge, will render to me in that day; but not only to me, but also to all who love his appearing”. We may say that Paul was well worthy of a crown of righteousness, well worthy of being recompensed for what he had done for Christ, but he would not claim this for himself alone, he would hold it out as the prospect for all who love His appearing. I trust that we all love the appearing of Jesus, and what a prospect it is that He is going to come first for His own. We were speaking earlier about the rapture, when the Lord Himself shall descend from heaven with an assembling shout, with archangel’s voice and with trump of God, and the dead in Christ shall rise first, and then the living will be caught up together with them to meet the Lord in the air (1 Thessalonians 4: 16, 17).

What a comfort it is to think of these things! We are in a world where everything is changing; people are changing and standards declining; deterioration marks everything; but this great system with which we have to do does not change or alter, or become devalued or depreciate in any way. The One who is the centre of it is the Same yesterday and today and to the ages to come. He is the righteous Judge who has laid up the crown of righteousness for us and He will render it to us in that day. It is not far distant now. It has been the hope of His own right down the ages from the time when He was taken into heaven and the word came, “This Jesus who has been taken up from you into heaven, shall thus come in the manner in which ye have beheld him going into heaven”, Acts 1: 11. This is what His own are looking for, and then the glorious matter of His shining forth, His coming to reign, which will follow soon after. What a time, and what a prospect, and what a Master to serve!

May we all be encouraged then as we think of these things. May we all be serving Him, and may we know this blessed One as our Saviour and as our Lord. He would desire to have us all engaged in His service. Maybe we cannot do very much; indeed, as it says, “We are unprofitable bondman; we have done what it was our duty to do”, Luke 17: 10. That is what Paul would say of himself, and yet he laboured more abundantly than all. The Lord would seek our allegiance and our service, and He would assure us of His love for each one of us, His interest in us, His desire and His ability to bring us right through to the end. May we be encouraged then, for His name’s sake.

articles.title: “I WILL RENDER TO THEE ON MY COMING BACK”
articles.author: M.P.

paragraphs.text: The inn to which the good Samaritan brought the wounded man is a well-known picture of the assembly, the loving circle of saints where the rescued one finds warm acceptance and affectionate care. That results from the blessed activity of the Holy Spirit, that wondrous divine Person who has stooped in grace to undertake the manifold services suggested by that expression, ‘the innkeeper’. Into His faithful hands the departing Rescuer has entrusted the beloved subjects of His own saving work—a fine touch of what we have in that sublime closing discourse of our Lord in John chapters 14 to 16. Now we know that the divine Comforter, guiding us into all the truth, “shall not speak from himself” but, as the Lord says, “He shall receive of mine”,

(John 16: 13, 14), receive of that exhaustless and immeasurable wealth—“All things that the Father has are mine”—of the unsearchable riches of the Christ, to make us rich and joyous, to produce holy feelings of love and admiration for the blessed Person of the Son in our hearts, to occupy us with His glory and to transform us accordingly.

Therefore we find that the innkeeper not only received the two denarii to spend for the rescued one, but is granted, so to say, a ‘blank cheque’ to be able to afford the best for healing and welfare. And there is a promise—“Whatsoever thou shalt expend more, I will render to thee on my coming back”. The complete fulfilment of that is no doubt still future but, as we know—blessed experience! our glorious and adorable Lord comes back even now into the circle of His own on that unique occasion on His day to receive the homage, worship, and affection of His saints, to make them feel His love and enjoy the unspeakable blessings of union with Him, all being actuated by the wondrous divine operations of the holy Comforter. And thus it becomes Christ’s part to “render to thee”. He imparts to the hearts of the saints, as united to Himself, His own feelings of love and gratefulness to the blessed Holy Spirit so that through them rich streams of response in praise and worship flow to extol the glorious Person and magnificent work of the divine Comforter who thus receives through the assembly His recompense in the power of her Head’s own perfect and peerlessly precious affections.

Lord Jesus Christ Thy lovers far and near
All call for Thee,
We long to see Thy face and hear Thy shout
Of victory,
To see Thee as Thou art in glory bright,
Th’assembly with Thee for Thine own delight.
The universe will then respond with joy
And liberty,
And all with breath will find their blest employ
In praising Thee;
Ten thousand thousand voices join as one
And by Thee rise to worship God alone.
Help us then, Lord, with Thee e’en now to be
With single eye,
Midst deep’ning darkness serve Thee faithfully
Where Thou didst die,
Thy suffering love to which we owe our all
Binding together those who on Thee call.
Melbourne, 1977
NOURISHING AND CHERISHING We received an impression in a reading as to the blessedness of Christ’s service to the assembly described in Ephesians 5: 29—He “nourishes and cherishes it”. The richest

experience of this cherishing is as we are restfully in the embrace of Christ’s love at the Supper “His left hand is under my head, And his right hand doth embrace me”. Song of Solomon 2: 6. At the same time we are nourished as we receive fresh impressions of the glory and grace of His Person.

This association of nourishing and cherishing gives a rich sense of the setting in which we receive the ministry that proceeds constantly from Christ for our nourishment. As it comes, whatever the occasion, we are conscious of being tenderly cherished by Him. The two things are simultaneous; as He nourishes us by a fresh ministration of food and enlightenment. He is embracing His assembly, the object of His love. This is the setting in which ministry is most effective.

Chapter 13 (of 1 Corinthians) brings in a point of the very last moment, and that is what our true measure is for the assembly—any man’s capability, his measure for the assembly is made plain enough in this chapter … Love is his measure. A man is only really qualified for the assembly in the measure in which he is formed in the divine nature.
